Violino piccolo 為巴洛克時期提琴家族的小型高音弦樂器。1613年: The violino piccolo is a small high-pitched string instrument of the Baroque violin family. Girolamo Amati of Cremona made one in 1613, and there is evidence of its use around Leipzig between 1650 and 1750; an example by the Amati brothers is held at the National Music Museum in Vermillion, South Dakota, and Johann Sebastian Bach's Brandenburg Concerto No. 1 also calls for it. After the construction of the violin changed in the Rococo period, the standard violin could play many of the high parts, and the instrument was no longer necessary. A soprano violin in the modern new violin family has a similar tuning, but it has not become standard.

The vibration of the strings sets the body resonating and produces rich overtones, so that the tone has plenty of layers. The bass is relatively thin, and not as heavy and warm as the cello's. Compared with an ordinary violin, this instrument is smaller and its pitch sharper and more delicate, its volume slightly less, but its treble carries further. Its tone comes near the lightness of a soprano flute, yet keeps the singing quality and warmth of a string instrument. In the Baroque period it was often used for accompaniment and ornamental passages, and could create a distinctive high register in an ensemble. Whether solo or in ensemble, the violin can show a refined and elegant sound.

The violino piccolo is a chordophone of the European Baroque period, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.322-71. It is close in form to the violin but smaller, and its usual tuning is a minor third or a perfect fourth above the standard violin. The well-known example by the Amati brothers shows a clear conceptual correspondence between the dimensions of its body, neck and fretboard and those of the standard violin. The instrument was used in Bach's Brandenburg Concerto No. 1; when the Rococo period began, the standard violin could play the higher register, and the violino piccolo was no longer considered necessary.
